newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Nov 14.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Nov 14.

text.p: The pilot of a Saudi Arabian jumbo jet involved in Wednesday's midair collision over northern India managed to avoid crashing into a village, a witness said on Wednesday night.

NZ First leader Winston Peters expects to take independent economic advice into Thursday's coalition talks, but is keeping the identity of his advisers secret. Peters expected some significant papers to be delivered by Thursday morning, but said commercial confidentiality prevented him saying who was

providing them. NZ First and Labour negotiators met for two-and-a-half hours on Wednsday, which was half an hour less than NZ First and National spent in discussions earlier in the day. Labour leader Helen Clark said that was because Labour and NZ First had fewer disagreements than NZ First and National. Peters said negotiations with both parties were now "a long way down the track".
The planned stadium on Wellington's railyards would be a world leader, a good neighbour and the safest place in town during an earthquake, stadium designer Rod Sheard said on Wednesday.

NZ First's five Maori electorate MPs needed to make sure they did not dominate the party and make it too Maori in character, one of them has warned. Te Tai Rawhiti MP John Delamere said the party's five Maori electorate MPs were "potentially huge" in their influence within the party's 17-MP caucus. "We five must never forget that we are part of a party as well as being Maori."

Business in the Wellington region is being badly hit by the three-month-long election doldrums and delay in forming a government, according to a Wellington Regional Chamber of Commerce Survey. Chamber policy analyst David Barnes said several companies had reported turnover falls of a quarter to a third becuase of the election doldrums. The worst case was one firm which reported a 50 percent fall in turnover. "There may even be the odd business going under because of the lack of confidence," Barnes said. There was normally a business lull before an election, but that lull had continued, Barnes said. The seasonal pattern of "quite bouyant" activity among retailers at this time had not shown up.

Sir Ron Brierley's foray in Colonial Motors paid off on Wednesday when the company announced a return of capital of 40 cents a share at Wednesday's annual general meeting in Wellington. The tax-free payout will be made in April after an extraordinary general meeting and approval by the High Court. The return of capital will see $12.37 million returned to shareholders, including over $4 million to Brierley's Guiness Peat Group.

Apple Fields shares soared 11 cents to 63 cents on Wednesday after the listed Cantebury grower threatened to rip up its trees and convert its orchards into residential properties. Chairman Murray Valentine said if the Apple and Pear Board did not approve Apple Fields' application to market its own export fruit in the coming season, the orchards would close at the end of the months and the company would turn to residential property and investment.
Comalco managing director Kerry McDonald has been named chairman of the Bank of New Zealand board.
Wreckage and burning bodies from the Saudi Arabian Airlines Boeing 747 were spread over six kilometres of fields in rural north India after the world's worst mid-air collision claimed 350 lives.

Tranz Rail and Auckland City Council negotiators have struck a last-minute deal to clear a major stumbling block from the $1.5 billion Britomart transport and building project. But an agreement on the rail company's occupancy of the proposed underground transport centre leaves many other issues unresolved as councillors prepare to vote on the project on Thursday nught. Among these issues, is a failure by the city council to seek environmental approvals for a rail tunnel into the centre.

Prime Minister Jim Bolger held a brief meeting on Wednesday with the Zulu leader Chief Mangosuthu Buthelezi discussing developments in South Africa, Zaire and Nigeria. The meeting lasted about 15 minutes.

The compulsory superannuation savings package which NZ First campaigned on would limit individuals' life choices and funnel investment offshore, says Infometrics economist Philip Wrigley. Wrigley, who produced an analysis of the various party manifestos during the election, said on Wednesday that he could NZ First leader Winston Peters on Thursday night indicated that he might sacrifice the party's compulsory supperannuation policy in return for a strategy to encourage long-term savings. Asked if he would be willing to give away the compulsory super scheme for a long-term savings strategy, Peters said: "In all topics you have to be prepared sometines to give a little to actually gain a lot and we have approached each subject that way. You cannot expect to go into talks and get everything you want." Peters belives a national savings strategy would create a base from which to boost investment in New Zealand, reducing its dependence on foreign capital. see no rationale for the scheme.

New Zealand icons Tip Top Ice Cream and Tegel Foods have been put up for sale in a worldwide tender by the internatiional food giant Heinz-Wattie. The move follows this week's consolidation of Wattie's businesses, which left both assets outside the core New Zealand operations. Sources said the assets were together thought to be worth as much as $500 million. Both have a controlling market share, with Tip Top holding about 80 percent share of the national ice cream market and Tegel around 70 percent of chicken sales. A sales process is expected to be completed by the first quarter of next year. A public offer may also be considered.

Enerco New Zealand added a further $4 million to its debt-free balance sheet on Wednesday and said it was still looking for acquisitions. The gas utility, which serves homes and businesses in Auckland, Wellington and Hawkes Bay boosted after-tax profit for the September half-year by 29 percent to $12.9 million.
Richina Pacific has traded ahead of budget since its June balance date in what is traditionally a slow half, chairman Jim Syme told the annual meeting in Auckland on Wednesday.
